paras: The Mendota mob threat against a burglar was an incident at Mendota, Illinois, reported in October 1881, in which a mob put a noose around the neck of a man accused of burglary and made him choose between hanging and promising to plead guilty. The man promised, and the mob dispersed without killing him. The story survives only as a short unattributed paragraph that newspapers ran with an ironic comment on the mob's idea of justice.

According to the paragraph, the man had not yet been brought to court and was due to be "arraigned" on the burglary charge. A mob at Mendota placed a noose around his neck and gave him "his choice between hanging and promising to plead guilty when arraigned in court." He agreed, and "the lynchers" then dispersed. The item gives no date, no names, no number for the mob, no setting and no race for anyone involved.
No report of the man's arraignment, plea or trial, or of any arrest of members of the mob, appears in the coverage.

The earliest copy found ran on October 27, 1881, in the Daily Globe's "Globelets" column of brief items, between notes on Mrs. Garfield and the Irish Times. Its closing line was ironic, saying the lynchers, "having thus succeeded in preventing a fair trial, dispersed without murdering the criminal." Nearly three weeks later The Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, printed the same paragraph among other filler items, but its version read "having thus succeeded in having a fair trial," a change that blunted the original irony. Neither paper credited a source or added any local detail, and no Illinois report of the incident was found.
The two copies agree on every fact of the incident and differ only in the comment on the mob's purpose, where the earlier Daily Globe wording, "preventing a fair trial," is more likely the original.

reader.title: Mendota mob threat against a burglar (1881)
bases: A mob, called 'lynchers', put a noose around an accused burglar's neck and threatened to hang him unless he promised to plead guilty, then dispersed without killing him (A1, A3).

No one was killed: the mob 'dispersed without murdering' the man after he promised to plead guilty (A1, A3). The mob acted without lawful authority over an alleged burglary, but its size is not given.
Both items are copies of one unattributed exchange paragraph (A1, A3); no independent or local report was found.

framing.detail: The Daily Globe ran the item in its 'Globelets' column with the ironic comment that the lynchers had succeeded 'in preventing a fair trial' and 'dispersed without murdering the criminal'.
The Silver State reprinted the paragraph as filler, with the comment altered to 'having a fair trial', which blunts or reverses the irony.
